name: Cocaine Embryofetopathy

ethnicAssociations: Higher prevalence reported in urban populations with increased maternal cocaine use

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Cocaine Embryofetopathy

criteria.description: Confirmed maternal cocaine use during pregnancy by history or toxicology
Presence of characteristic facial abnormalities including short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, and flattened nasal bridge
Intrauterine growth restriction or low birth weight not explained by other causes
Evidence of central nervous system dysfunction such as irritability, tremors, or developmental delay
Presence of congenital heart defects or vascular abnormalities

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Confirmed maternal cocaine use plus presence of at least two major criteria including characteristic facial dysmorphology and growth restriction
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical and supported by maternal history and exclusion of other teratogenic exposures

laboratory: Positive toxicology screen for cocaine metabolites in maternal or neonatal urine or meconium
imaging: Brain ultrasound or MRI showing cerebral atrophy or ventriculomegaly
genetic: No specific genetic markers; diagnosis based on exposure and clinical features
other: Maternal history of cocaine use during pregnancy
Neonatal behavioral assessment showing irritability and hypertonia

distinguishingFeatures: History of maternal alcohol use rather than cocaine
Characteristic facial features differ (e.g., smooth philtrum, thin upper lip)
Growth restriction and neurodevelopmental delay overlap but facial phenotype distinct
Withdrawal symptoms from opioids or other substances
Absence of characteristic facial dysmorphology seen in cocaine embryofetopathy

redFlags: Confirmed maternal cocaine use during pregnancy
Severe intrauterine growth restriction with no other cause
Presence of characteristic facial dysmorphic features
references: Lester BM, Lagasse LL. Children of addicted women. J Addict Dis. 2010;29(2):259-276.
Behnke M, Smith VC; Committee on Substance Abuse; Committee on Fetus and Newborn. Prenatal substance abuse: short- and long-term effects on the exposed fetus. Pediatrics. 2013;131(3):e1009-e1024.
